published.title: Why Dividing by Zero Is Undefined
published.signature: Why is division by zero undefined in ordinary arithmetic, and why do some number systems assign it a meaning anyway? The operation a divided by 0, its relation to multiplicative inverses, and the difference between a limit that approaches a value and a value that is actually assigned. Division by b is multiplication by the reciprocal of b, and zero has no reciprocal in the real numbers; limits describe approach, not the value at the forbidden point.

published.title: Why Is the Sky Blue? Rayleigh Scattering Explained
published.signature: Why does a clear sky appear blue, and why does the same scattering process make a setting Sun look red or orange? The wavelength dependence of Rayleigh scattering, how it redistributes sunlight across the sky, and why the long path through the atmosphere near the horizon removes blue light from the direct solar beam. Air molecules scatter short visible wavelengths much more efficiently than long ones, roughly as the inverse fourth power of wavelength, so scattered blue light dominates the sky while transmitted red light dominates the low Sun.

published.title: Why Does Ice Float on Water?
published.signature: Why is solid water less dense than liquid water, and what does that anomaly imply for natural bodies of water? The molecular geometry of the water molecule, the open hydrogen-bonded lattice of ice, the density maximum of liquid water near 4 °C, and the ecological consequences of ice floating instead of sinking. Water molecules can donate and accept hydrogen bonds in four directions, so freezing locks them into an open tetrahedral network that occupies more volume than the liquid; density, not molecular weight, decides whether ice floats.
published.primary_keyword: why does ice float on water

published.title: How Does CRISPR-Cas9 Find Its Target?
published.signature: How does the Cas9 protein use a guide RNA and a PAM sequence to locate a specific DNA site, and why does the search sometimes accept the wrong one? The roles of the guide RNA spacer, the PAM, local DNA unwinding, seed-first proofreading, nuclease activation, and the kinetic and structural reasons off-target sites can still be cut. Cas9 narrows the search with a short PAM, tests candidate sites by unwinding the duplex, and activates its scissors only after sufficient guide complementarity, so target recognition is a staged kinetic proofread rather than a single exact string match.
published.primary_keyword: how does CRISPR-Cas9 find its target

published.title: Why Does the Moon Always Show the Same Face?
published.signature: How does tidal friction force a moon to rotate once per orbit, and why does the resulting lock still let us see more than half of the lunar surface? The difference between rotation and orbital motion, the tidal bulge raised by Earth, the torque that slows the Moon's spin, the energy budget that makes the lock stable, and the librations that reveal about 59 percent of the lunar surface. Earth's gravity stretches the Moon, and the lagging tidal bulge exerts a torque that drains rotational energy until the Moon's spin period equals its orbital period; at that point the bulge points steadily at Earth and the torque vanishes.
published.primary_keyword: why does the moon always show the same face

published.title: How Do We Know the Universe Is Expanding?
published.signature: What observations show that the universe is expanding, and how do redshift and the distance ladder turn that expansion into a measurable rate? The meaning of cosmological redshift, the distance ladder used to calibrate Hubble's law, the difference between expansion and motion through space, the discovery of accelerating expansion, and the current Hubble tension. Space itself stretches between gravitationally bound systems, so light from distant galaxies arrives with longer wavelengths and a recession speed proportional to distance; the proportionality constant is the Hubble constant, and its change over time encodes the universe's matter, radiation, and dark-energy content.
published.primary_keyword: how do we know the universe is expanding

published.title: Where Do the Elements Come From?
published.signature: Which processes produced the elements, and how do astronomers know which elements came from the Big Bang, which came from ordinary stars, and which required explosions? Big Bang nucleosynthesis, hydrogen and helium fusion in stars, the triple-alpha process, the onion-shell burning of massive stars, the iron endpoint, and the neutron-capture processes that make elements heavier than iron. Fusion releases energy only until the iron peak, so stars build elements up to iron in their cores and release the rest through supernovae and neutron-star mergers, where rapid neutron capture can assemble the heaviest nuclei.
published.primary_keyword: where do the elements come from

published.title: Why Is the Halting Problem Undecidable?
published.signature: Why can no algorithm decide, for every possible program and input, whether that program eventually halts? The definition of a Turing machine, the assumption of a halting decider, the diagonal construction that derives a contradiction from that assumption, and what undecidability does and does not imply in practice. A universal halting decider would allow a program to ask what the decider says about itself and then do the opposite, producing a contradiction; since the construction is valid for any candidate decider, no such decider can exist.
published.primary_keyword: why is the halting problem undecidable

published.title: Why Do Earthquakes Happen Where They Do?
published.signature: Why are earthquakes concentrated along plate boundaries rather than spread evenly across the planet, and what makes the rock there fail? The geometry of tectonic plates, the difference between divergent, convergent, and transform boundaries, the elastic rebound cycle that stores and releases strain, and the reasons subduction zones produce the largest earthquakes and tsunamis. Earthquakes occur where moving plates lock against one another and elastic strain accumulates in brittle rock; when the stress exceeds friction and strength, the rock slips suddenly and radiates seismic waves.

published.title: How Do Scientists Recover DNA from Ancient Bones?
published.signature: What happens to DNA after an organism dies, and how do researchers separate authentic ancient fragments from contamination and assemble them into a genome? The chemical decay of DNA after death, the structure of ancient fragments, the clean-room and contamination controls, the role of molecular baits and high-throughput sequencing, and the limits and ethics of ancient-genome research. Ancient DNA survives only as short, damaged fragments, so authenticity depends on chemical signatures of decay, sterile handling, and computational mapping that distinguishes endogenous fragments from contamination.
published.primary_keyword: how do scientists recover dna from ancient bones

published.title: Why Is There No Largest Prime Number?
published.signature: How can we prove that the sequence of prime numbers never ends, without finding an explicit formula for the next prime? The definition of a prime, the structure of Euclid's proof by contradiction, the distinction between the constructed number and a new prime, an example, and why the argument does not produce a practical formula for generating primes. Given any finite list of primes, multiplying them and adding one produces a number that is not divisible by any prime on the list, so some prime outside the list must exist; therefore no finite list can contain all primes.
published.primary_keyword: why is there no largest prime number

published.title: How Do Plants Turn Sunlight into Food?
published.signature: How does a plant capture light energy and use it to build sugar from carbon dioxide and water, and where does the oxygen come from? The structure of the chloroplast, the light reactions that split water and produce ATP and NADPH, the Calvin cycle that fixes carbon dioxide with Rubisco, the overall equation and energy budget, and the reasons efficiency is limited in real leaves. Light-driven electron transport in the thylakoid membrane splits water, releases oxygen, and stores energy in ATP and NADPH, which the Calvin cycle then uses to reduce carbon dioxide into sugar.
published.primary_keyword: how do plants turn sunlight into food

published.title: Why Can't Computers Generate Truly Random Numbers?
published.signature: How can a deterministic machine produce numbers that look random, and what does it take to make those numbers genuinely unpredictable? The difference between pseudorandom, cryptographically secure, and true random numbers, how seeds and deterministic algorithms generate sequences, where physical entropy comes from, and why statistical tests alone cannot prove unpredictability. A deterministic program can stretch a short random seed into a long sequence that passes statistical tests, but true unpredictability requires an unpredictable physical source that an observer cannot reproduce.
published.primary_keyword: why can't computers generate truly random numbers

published.title: Why Is the Ocean Salty?
published.signature: Where do the dissolved ions in seawater come from, and why has the ocean not simply become saltier and saltier over geological time? The weathering of continental rock, hydrothermal exchange at mid-ocean ridges, the composition of seawater, the ocean's salt budget over millions of years, and why salinity varies between seas and with depth. Seawater is salty because rock-derived ions accumulate in a reservoir with a long mixing time, while removal by sedimentation, sea spray, and hydrothermal circulation keeps the total concentration roughly steady over geological time.

published.title: How Does Quantum Sensing Beat Classical Limits?
published.signature: What limits a classical measurement, and how do quantum states allow sensors to surpass the standard quantum limit? The standard quantum limit and shot noise, the role of superposition in atomic clocks and interferometers, entanglement and squeezing as resources, and the practical applications of quantum sensors in navigation, geology, and fundamental physics. Quantum sensors use a quantum probe whose phase or state accumulates information about an external field, and they manipulate uncertainty so that the measurement noise falls below the standard quantum limit set by independent particles.
published.primary_keyword: how does quantum sensing beat classical limits

pending.title: Why Do Bridges Have Expansion Joints?
pending.signature: How much does a bridge change length with temperature, and how do expansion joints and bearings accommodate that movement without weakening the structure? The physics of thermal expansion, a numerical estimate for a long steel or concrete span, the difference between joints and bearings, the consequences of restrained movement, and the other sources of bridge movement that joints must handle. Materials change length when their temperature changes, and a long bridge accumulates enough movement that the structure must be allowed to slide or flex at designed locations instead of being rigidly restrained.

pending.title: Why Does a Spinning Top Stay Upright?
pending.signature: Why does rotation stabilize a top against gravity, and why does the axis precess instead of simply falling? The definition of angular momentum and torque, the vector relationship between them, why a torque perpendicular to angular momentum changes its direction rather than its magnitude, the resulting precession, and why friction eventually brings the top down. Gravity exerts a torque that is perpendicular to the top's angular momentum, and a perpendicular torque rotates the angular momentum vector instead of reducing it, so the axis sweeps around in precession while the spin keeps the top from falling quickly.
